title: The Odd Women: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Three Women at the Crossroads

utterances.text: Welcome to The Odd Women Unpacked — a close, argued, thoroughly enjoyed reading of George Gissing's 1893 novel.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be living inside one of the most searching novels ever written about women, work, and what it means to be free.
Gissing's title is a joke with a bitter edge — the 'odd women' are the surplus women of Victorian England, statistically left over, unmarried, economically precarious.
But Gissing does something extraordinary with that premise — he turns surplus into argument, and argument into drama.
Three brilliant people are joining me today, and I want to introduce them properly, because each of them brings a completely different ear to this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Gissing as a performer who hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose literary judgements carry the weight of a very long, very well-read life — he will tell us what the novel is actually about, beneath all our clever theories.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as X-rays of power — he'll show us the skeleton beneath Gissing's Victorian flesh.
Let's begin where Gissing begins — with a family portrait that is really an economic sentence of death.
What strikes me first — always, every time I return to this novel — is the opening movement's terrible efficiency.
Gissing gives us Dr. Madden and his six daughters in the first chapter, and within a few pages that father is dead and the daughters are simply — adrift.
There's no melodrama about it, which is the masterstroke.
Gissing simply notes that the daughters have been educated as if husbands were guaranteed, and then quietly removes that guarantee.
It's like watching a conjuror remove the tablecloth — except all the china smashes.
And the daughters we follow — Monica, Virginia, Alice — are not stupid women.
That's what makes it so painful to watch them flail within systems entirely designed for their failure.
Oliver is right about the efficiency, though I'd describe what Gissing achieves rather differently.
The Madden sisters are not victims of a system, primarily — they are inheritors of a particular kind of moral failure.
Their father is a decent man, affectionate, but he has been culpably imprudent.
He has raised daughters without preparing them for the reality of their position.
Now — Gissing does not sentimentalise this.
He is too good a novelist for that.
But I think it matters enormously that the novel's catastrophe begins in parental failure — in a failure of love to become wisdom.
That is a very different diagnosis from Oliver's, and from Daniel's, I suspect.
Edmund, I'd say Dr. Madden's failure and the system's failure are the same failure — the system produces men like Dr. Madden.
He is not an aberration — he is the norm.
Middle-class Victorian men routinely failed to secure their daughters' futures because the ideology of femininity actively discouraged women from learning how to secure it themselves.
What Gissing maps in those opening chapters is the material consequence of that ideology — these women have no trade, no capital, no recourse.
Virginia descends into secret drinking.
Alice is worn down to a kind of exhausted resignation.
Monica — the youngest, the most vital — makes the worst calculation available to her, and marries Widdowson.
These are not personal failures — they are economic destinies, wearing the costume of personal choice.
And set against the Madden sisters — almost as a deliberate structural contrast — we have Rhoda Nunn and Mary Barfoot.
These are women who have, in their different ways, refused the available destinies.
Oliver — how do you read that contrast in the novel's architecture?
It's the novel's great structural gamble, and Gissing wins it, I think, though it took me a second reading to feel entirely sure.
Mary Barfoot and Rhoda run a typewriting school — training women for the new clerical economy.
And from one angle that sounds very prosaic — almost satirically mundane as a vehicle for feminist argument.
But Gissing makes it feel like a revolutionary cell operating inside a hostile society.
These women are actually doing something — and that 'actually' is doing enormous weight in the novel.
Against the drift and dissolution of the Maddens, Barfoot and Nunn represent a kind of willed, precarious, magnificent self-invention.
I'll allow that Mary Barfoot is a genuinely admirable creation — Gissing gives her a warmth and a pragmatic intelligence that is very attractive.
She believes in her cause, but she is also a woman of the world — she understands that causes without economics are merely sermons.
Rhoda Nunn is a rather more complicated proposition for me.
Her rigidity — her insistence on an almost programmatic independence — strikes me as a different kind of imprudence from Dr. Madden's, but imprudence nonetheless.
Dr. Johnson would have recognised her type immediately — the person so committed to a principle that they are incapable of being surprised by human nature.
And of course, Gissing — very shrewdly — arranges for Everard Barfoot to walk through her door and complicate all that.
What I find most remarkable about this novel's opening is the precision of Gissing's social geometry.
He places these two worlds — the Maddens' slow-motion catastrophe and Barfoot and Nunn's embattled project — at opposite ends of the same social stratum.
They are not class enemies.
They are women of the same respectable poverty, facing the same foreclosed horizon — but responding to it with utterly different wills.
And that is Gissing's argument in miniature — not that individual will is irrelevant, but that individual will is where ideology does its most intimate damage.
To break with the available script, as Rhoda has done, costs something — Gissing is not sentimental about that cost.
And that cost — what it actually means to live Rhoda Nunn's kind of independence — is exactly where we're headed next.
Because Rhoda is not just a model of the emancipated woman — she is also a woman in the grip of something she hasn't fully reckoned with.
After the break, we'll look at Rhoda Nunn's uncompromising stand — and ask whether what looks like principle might sometimes be armour.

segments.title: The Weight of Independence: Rhoda Nunn's Uncompromising Stand

utterances.text: We've been thinking about three women standing at crossroads — each one facing a different version of the same impossible question.
Now I want to put one figure at the very centre of our lens: Rhoda Nunn, the woman who seems to have answered that question — and answered it with something close to ferocity.
Rhoda Nunn is one of those characters you meet and immediately want to perform — not because she's theatrical, but because she's so completely herself.
Every line she speaks has this bracing quality — like cold water thrown in your face and you're grateful for it.

Gissing gives her this magnificent set piece early on where she declares, in effect, that marriage is the enemy of women's development — not as a polemic, but as a simple statement of observable fact.
And what makes it extraordinary on the page — and even more so aloud — is how utterly calm she is.
There's no shrillness, no martyrdom — just this clear-eyed certainty that the world has arranged itself absurdly, and she has decided not to participate in the absurdity.
I think Oliver is right about the calm — and that calm is precisely what troubles me about her, in the most productive sense.
Rhoda is not a satirical target for Gissing — he clearly admires her.
And yet he is honest enough — or perhaps cruel enough — to show us the cost.
Her great speech to Mary Barfoot about the 'odd women' — those surplus women whom society has no designated role for — is stirring, genuinely stirring.
But Gissing places it in a life that is, for much of the novel, conspicuously unlived — in the domestic and emotional sense.
Whether one calls that sacrifice or impoverishment depends rather on one's values, I suppose.
I'd push back on 'unlived' — because that framing smuggles in the assumption that a life oriented around independence and work is somehow less than a life oriented around a husband.
What Gissing is actually mapping, with great precision, is the material conditions that make Rhoda's position both necessary and radical.
The typewriting school that she and Mary Barfoot run is not a hobby — it is an intervention in the labour market on behalf of women who would otherwise have no economic existence.
Rhoda's personal stance and the school's institutional purpose are the same argument made at two different scales.
When she tells Everard Barfoot that she wants no part of the conventional marriage arrangement, she is not being personally eccentric — she is being structurally consistent.
But there is an Everard Barfoot problem, isn't there — and it's delicious.
Gissing has the audacity to give Rhoda — the most principled woman in the novel — the most compelling man.
Everard is clever, he is charming, he is genuinely interested in ideas — and he proceeds to test Rhoda in the most systematic way imaginable.
He even proposes what he calls a 'free union' — marriage in spirit but not in law — as if removing the legal chain would make the existential one vanish.
And you can feel Rhoda — feel her, on the page — genuinely wavering.
Gissing does not let her off easily, which is what makes her final refusal so hard-won.
That wavering is the most humanly truthful thing in the novel, I would argue.
Gissing understands — as all the great novelists understand — that conviction is not the same as immunity to feeling.
What is tested in Rhoda is not her intelligence — no one doubts her intelligence — but her will.
And there is a passage, when Rhoda reflects on what she calls the 'dread of an unoccupied future,' that I find genuinely affecting.
'The dread of an unoccupied future was one of the results of her education.'
That is Gissing acknowledging that her independence is not a natural condition — it was made, effortfully, against considerable resistance.
And things that are made can, in principle, be unmade.
And this is where Everard Barfoot becomes ideologically fascinating rather than merely romantically interesting.
He presents himself as a progressive — a man who has moved beyond the tyranny of convention.
But the free union he proposes still centres him — his comfort, his freedom from legal obligation, his ability to leave.
Rhoda sees this, I think, even when she is most drawn to him.
There is that extraordinary exchange where she tells him, in effect, that to accept his terms would be to prove that all her principles were merely waiting for the right man to dissolve them.
Gissing phrases it with characteristic bluntness: 'I thought I was above such weaknesses.'
That 'thought' — past tense, conditional, shaken — is doing enormous work.
It is Gissing's honest admission that ideological clarity and emotional reality do not always occupy the same person peacefully.
And then there is the scene in the Lakeland countryside — which Gissing, bless him, uses with no subtlety whatsoever and every possible effectiveness.
The landscape is doing precisely what Victorian landscapes do — loosening the stays of civilisation, inviting the characters to be something other than their social roles.
And Rhoda, out there in the open air, is closer to yielding than at any other point in the novel.
It's gloriously uncomfortable to read — because you want her to yield, and simultaneously you know it would be a kind of defeat.
Gissing engineers that ambivalence with the skill of a novelist who is himself entirely unresolved on the question.
I want to say something in Everard's partial defence, if I may.
He is not, I think, a villain — he is a man who has constructed a philosophy of personal freedom and is genuinely surprised to find it colliding with someone who has constructed a more rigorous one.
The novel's real sting comes when Rhoda discovers — or believes she discovers — his entanglement with Agnes Brissenden.
Because that is where the theoretical becomes personal — and personal wounds have a way of hardening positions that might otherwise have softened.
What Rhoda ends the novel with is not, I would argue, serene independence — it is independence purchased at the price of a very particular grief.
I don't dispute the grief — but I think we should be careful not to read the grief as Gissing's verdict on her choices.
Look at what surrounds her at the novel's close: Monica dead, Widdowson broken, the Madden sisters crushed one by one by economic dependence.
Every woman in this novel who chose the conventional path has paid a price that dwarfs Rhoda's.
And the school goes on — the work continues — young women are being trained for economic life.
Rhoda's grief is real, but it is also, structurally, the price the novel asks her to pay to prove she is human rather than merely symbolic.
That is very well put — 'human rather than merely symbolic' — because Gissing really does refuse to make her a saint.
He gives her vanity, he gives her occasional cruelty — particularly in how she handles Monica — and he gives her this absolutely remorseless capacity to judge.
There's a moment where she reflects on Monica's situation with something that is not quite sympathy — it's closer to impatience.
As if Monica has wasted a resource — herself — that Rhoda would have deployed more efficiently.
It is almost cold — and yet you understand it perfectly.
And that cold understanding — and what it costs the one who holds it — is something Gissing returns to again and again in this novel.
Which brings us to Monica herself — the woman who made the opposite choice, and what that choice actually looked like from the inside.

segments.title: A Loveless Bargain: Monica's Surrender and Survival

utterances.text: We've been looking at Rhoda Nunn's fierce refusal to compromise — her almost militant independence.
But Gissing places another woman at the centre of this novel whose path runs in almost the opposite direction.
Monica Madden — the youngest of the Madden sisters — chooses marriage, and Gissing gives us no illusions about what that choice costs her.
Monica is one of Gissing's most quietly devastating creations, and I think she's sometimes underestimated because she isn't combative.
She doesn't argue with the world — she tries to survive it.
She's trapped behind a draper's counter when we first meet her — exhausted, underpaid, her health already fraying.
And Gissing is unflinching about what the draper's trade does to young women's bodies and spirits.
When Widdowson comes along with his respectability and his income, the reader understands perfectly why Monica says yes.
Gissing makes sure we understand — and he makes sure we understand the tragedy of that understanding.
I think that's right, but I'd resist framing it purely as victimhood.
Monica has genuine romantic feeling — or at least the longing for it — and she brings a great deal of her own trouble upon herself.
There is a passage early in her courtship where Gissing tells us quite plainly that she does not love Widdowson.
She reflects that his manner of looking at her gave her a sense of satisfaction — the satisfaction, one feels, of being wanted rather than of wanting.
Gissing is not sentimental about this distinction.
Monica chooses comfort and escape — which is entirely human — but she chooses it with her eyes open, and that matters morally.
Eyes open — yes, but open to what choices, exactly?
Monica's alternatives are the draper's counter, or dependence on her sisters, or the slow grind of genteel poverty.
Gissing is extraordinarily precise about the economic arithmetic of her situation.
When she accepts Widdowson, she is not making a romantic error — she is executing a rational calculation with the limited variables available to her.
To call that a moral failing is, I'd suggest, to mistake the symptom for the disease.
I wouldn't call it a failing — I'd call it a compromise, which is a different thing.
And Gissing is, at his best, a novelist of compromises and their consequences.
What strikes me about Monica's marriage is not the wedding but what comes after — the creeping realisation that she has exchanged one cage for another.
Widdowson's house in Herne Hill is comfortable enough, but Gissing renders it with a kind of suffocating stillness.
Monica is not beaten or abused — she is simply watched, and controlled, and gradually extinguished.
That word — extinguished — is exactly right, and I think Gissing earns it through accumulation.
There's a marvellous, terrible scene where Monica simply wants to go out — to walk, to visit Mildred Vesper, to exist in the world.
And Widdowson's response is this extraordinary performance of wounded propriety.
He doesn't forbid her exactly — he suffers.
He makes his suffering so visible, so heavy in the room, that Monica's freedom becomes an act of cruelty in his framing.
Gissing understands that domestic tyranny rarely announces itself with a locked door — it announces itself with a long, reproachful silence.
And the ideology doing the work there is Widdowson's conception of what a wife is for.
He has a genuinely medieval notion — dressed up in Victorian respectability — that a wife is property to be protected, which is to say possessed.

There's a moment — and it's one of the most chilling in the novel — where Widdowson tells Monica something to the effect that a wife's place is her home, and that going out into the world is a kind of contamination.
Gissing gives Widdowson just enough self-awareness to make him pitiful rather than purely monstrous — which is the more disturbing choice.
Because a monster can be expelled from the story. A man who genuinely believes he loves his wife while destroying her — that's the novel's real horror.
And that's where Everard Barfoot enters the picture — because Monica's friendship with Barfoot becomes the fulcrum on which Widdowson's jealousy tips into genuine persecution.
Oliver, how do you read Gissing's handling of that relationship — is Monica reaching for escape, or for something she never had?
Both, I think — and Gissing is wise enough not to separate them.
Monica's attraction to Barfoot is partly intellectual — he talks to her as though her opinions matter, which Widdowson essentially never does.
But it's also the simple, terrible pull of being seen as a person rather than an appendage.
What I find so painful in the novel is that Gissing gives Monica a genuine moment of awakening — she glimpses a different kind of life — and then closes the door on it absolutely.
Her death in childbirth at the novel's end isn't melodrama. It's the logic of the system played out to its conclusion.
I want to push back on that slightly — not to exonerate the system, but to restore Monica's agency in the tragedy.
Gissing gives Monica opportunities — through Mary Barfoot's circle, through Rhoda's example — that she does not take.
She visits the typewriting school, she meets women who have carved out independence — and she retreats.
There is a timidity in Monica — a longing for the conventional shelter of marriage — that Gissing renders without contempt but also without false sympathy.
Her tragedy is not simply what is done to her — it is also the choices that close around her, some of which she closes herself.
I don't deny Monica's interiority — but I'd say we have to ask what 'agency' means for a woman with no financial independence and no professional training.
Rhoda Nunn can make her austere choices precisely because Mary Barfoot has created an institution that gives her economic ground to stand on.
Monica has no such ground. The retreat Edmund describes isn't timidity in any simple sense — it's the rational response to having nothing to retreat to.
Gissing himself understood this. He wrote Monica with a specificity and a tenderness that suggests he knew exactly what the novel was accusing.
And the baby — that detail is so precisely Gissing.
Monica gives birth to a child she will never raise, in a marriage that was always a kind of slow erasure.
And Widdowson survives — to grieve, to repent, probably to marry again.
Gissing gives the system its victory, and he gives Monica her death, and he doesn't flinch from either.
That's what separates him from a sentimentalist — he won't rescue his characters to spare the reader's feelings.
Monica's story ends in that terrible economy of loss — and Widdowson's jealousy, as you've all touched on, is at the heart of it.
Which brings us to the man himself — because Gissing lavishes a kind of dark comic attention on Widdowson's possessiveness that deserves its own reckoning.

segments.title: The Comic Misery of Widdowson's Possessiveness

utterances.text: We've been tracing the slow suffocation of Monica's marriage — the way her surrender was never quite complete, never quite peace.
Which brings us, rather naturally, to the man doing the suffocating — Edmund Widdowson, one of literature's great comic monsters.
Except, of course, he's not quite a monster — and that's precisely what makes him so uncomfortable to read.
Widdowson is a gift — an absolutely spectacular gift to any reader who enjoys watching a man destroy himself with his own anxiety.
He has retired on a modest income, he has no occupation, no real purpose — and then he acquires Monica, and she becomes the occupation.
He follows her through the streets of London. He watches the windows of her friends' houses. He times her return home to the minute.
And the extraordinary thing is that Gissing renders all of this with something very close to comedy — a comedy of absolute dread.
There's a passage where Widdowson essentially admits that his idea of a wife is a creature who exists entirely within the domestic sphere — who has no life that is not sanctioned by her husband.
He says something to the effect that a wife's place is her home, that women who go about independently are not behaving as women should.
And Gissing lets him say it with complete conviction — there's no authorial sneer. Widdowson believes every word.
I'd want to resist the word 'comedy' slightly — or at least to complicate it.
Widdowson is not a fool. He is a man of limited imagination who has made a catastrophic mistake — which is not quite the same thing.
He married a young woman thirty years his junior because he wanted warmth and companionship — perfectly human desires.
What he could not foresee — what his nature made it impossible for him to foresee — was that those desires would curdle into tyranny.
Gissing is actually quite generous to him in certain moments — Widdowson is capable of self-reproach, even tenderness.
He knows, in his clearer moments, that he is behaving unreasonably. He simply cannot stop.
That is not a comic figure — that is a tragic one. A man imprisoned by the very temperament he cannot shed.
Edmund's point about self-reproach is well-taken — but I think we need to be careful not to let Widdowson's occasional tenderness obscure what he actually represents.
His possessiveness is not simply a personality defect. It is the logical extension of a property relation.
He has purchased Monica's time, her body, her social presence — in the most literal sense available to Victorian law.
And when he follows her through the streets, when he interrogates her about every hour of her day — he is simply enforcing the terms of the contract.
What makes Gissing remarkable is that he shows us a man who genuinely believes he is acting out of love — while systematically destroying the person he claims to love.
That gap between self-image and material effect — that is the ideological core of the novel's critique of bourgeois marriage.
Daniel's right about the contract, and Edmund's right about the tragedy — but I'd argue Gissing holds all three registers simultaneously, which is the real trick.
Think about the surveillance episodes — Widdowson literally lurking outside the house in Chelsea where Monica visits Bevis.
He is skulking in the fog, watching a front door, a middle-aged man of independent means reduced to the condition of a private detective.
There is something almost Dickensian in that image — farcical and pitiable at once.
And yet the consequences for Monica are entirely real — every evening he interrogates her, every discrepancy in her account becomes a wound he presses.
Gissing won't let the comedy release the pressure. He keeps them both — the absurdity and the cruelty — in the same frame.
There's a scene I return to often — where Widdowson presents Monica with a programme of self-improvement.
He wants her to read serious books, to cultivate her mind — according to his prescription, naturally.
It is, in its way, a portrait of benevolent despotism — he genuinely believes he is improving her.
And Monica — bless her — endures it with a patience that Gissing describes as increasingly mechanical.
Her inner life has simply retreated beyond his reach. She answers his questions; she reads his books; she gives him nothing of herself.
It is a masterclass in the psychology of a trapped person — survival through a kind of interior emigration.
That phrase — interior emigration — is exactly right. And it points to something Gissing understands with unusual clarity.
Monica's resistance is necessarily invisible — because visible resistance would be punished.
She has no legal recourse, no economic independence, no support network outside the women she met before her marriage.
Her connection to Rhoda Nunn and the world of Wimpole Street represents the only imaginable alternative — and Widdowson, with his instinctive radar for threat, resents that connection bitterly.
He cannot name what he fears from those women — but he fears it. Women who have chosen not to be owned.
And there's the extraordinary irony — his jealousy of Bevis, which is at least partly warranted, is almost a distraction from the deeper threat.
Bevis is a romantic escapade — a fantasy. Rhoda Nunn and Mary Barfoot are a philosophy.
Widdowson can follow Monica to a house in Chelsea. He cannot follow her into a changed mind.
And that, I think, is where Gissing's comedy tips into something genuinely painful — the moment you realise that Widdowson has already lost, and doesn't know it yet.
Widdowson lost, and the institution of marriage itself in crisis — which leads us directly to our next question.
Because Gissing doesn't only diagnose the problem — he's testing whether any of his characters can actually escape it.
What happens when the women of Wimpole Street try to build something different — and what are the limits of what reform can actually achieve?

segments.title: Social Entrapment and the Limits of Reform

utterances.text: Widdowson's jealousy gave us one face of entrapment — a man who mistakes ownership for love.
But Gissing is doing something much larger in this novel — he's mapping a whole society in which escape routes for women are systematically closed off.
Let's turn to that broader question: social entrapment, and whether the novel believes reform is actually possible.
The novel is, at its structural core, an anatomy of blocked exits.
Gissing positions Rhoda Nunn and Mary Barfoot's typewriting school as the reform proposition — the thing the novel holds up and tests.
And what does it actually produce?
Monica Madden walks through that door, acquires a little economic foothold, and then the gravitational pull of marriage drags her straight back into the old system.
The school is not a solution — it's a temporary reprieve before the walls close in.
I would put it rather differently, and I think with greater fidelity to what the novel actually shows us.
Monica's return to the old system, as Daniel calls it, is not the failure of a social structure — it is the failure of Monica's own character under pressure.
She is romantically susceptible, she is impulsive, and she makes a choice — marriage to Widdowson — that her own intelligence ought to have warned her against.
Gissing is not indifferent to social conditions, I grant you that.
But he is first and foremost a novelist of moral psychology — of what people do with whatever freedom they do possess.
Edmund, I love that reading, but I think the novel rather cheats Monica out of the freedom you're attributing to her.
Think about where we first meet her — behind the counter of a draper's shop, exhausted, underpaid, surrounded by other young women in identical servitude.
Gissing gives us that world with extraordinary precision — the pettiness of the rules, the surveillance of the shop floor, the sheer grind of it.
And then Widdowson appears, and he is — whatever else you say about him — a way out of that shop.
Her choice, Edmund, is less a moral failure than a calculation made under conditions of near-desperation.
And that's the mechanism Gissing is so precise about — marriage as a labour market for women who have no other viable labour market.
Mary Barfoot says it almost in those terms at one point, in her lectures to the students at the school.
She speaks of women who are taught that marriage is the one respectable goal, and who are therefore helpless when marriage fails or never arrives.
That's the ideological apparatus Gissing is dismantling — the idea that female virtue consists in waiting to be chosen.
And the three Madden sisters at the beginning of the novel are the tragic proof of what happens when that ideology meets economic reality.
The Madden sisters are genuinely moving — I will not dispute that.
Their father's death leaves them utterly unprepared for independent life, and Gissing handles that with great tenderness and without sentimentality.
But I'd note that the father himself is a man of good intentions and catastrophic impracticality — he is not a villain of the system, he is a fond, foolish man.
Gissing is asking: what does it cost when an individual fails in his duty of care?
That is a moral question, not merely an economic one.
Both things can be true at once, surely — the father can be a well-meaning fool and the system can be merciless.
What Gissing does so brilliantly with the Madden sisters is show us the arithmetic of genteel poverty in close, unsparing detail.
Virginia drifting toward drink, Alice ageing into anxious religiosity, Monica making the desperate leap toward Widdowson.
Each sister is a variation on the same theme — what happens to a woman with no training, no capital, and a fading claim to respectability.
Gissing writes it almost like a naturalist cataloguing specimens — with great sympathy but also a kind of terrible scientific clarity.
And then there's Rhoda Nunn — who seems at first to be the novel's answer, the woman who has escaped.
What does the novel do with her as a figure of reformed womanhood?
Rhoda is fascinating precisely because she is the reform proposition embodied — and then Gissing subjects her to Everard Barfoot.
Barfoot is a man who professes progressive views about women — free unions, independence, modernity — and who uses those views as a more sophisticated instrument of seduction.
And Rhoda nearly falls.

What Gissing shows us is that even an intellectually emancipated woman, operating in the most favourable circumstances available, remains vulnerable to a man who has learned the language of emancipation.
The system doesn't just operate through brutes like Widdowson — it operates through charming progressives like Barfoot.
Barfoot is a wonderful creation — one of those characters who is technically on the right side of every argument and yet somehow leaves you feeling soiled.
His courtship of Rhoda has this quality of a chess game in which only he knows the rules.
He proposes the free union specifically because he knows Rhoda's ideology makes it hard for her to refuse without seeming inconsistent.
It is a trap constructed entirely from her own principles.
That is extraordinary writing — genuinely cruel in its intelligence.
I'll defend Barfoot on one point, if I may — not morally, but structurally.
He does eventually offer Rhoda genuine marriage, and she refuses him.
What Gissing then gives us is Rhoda at the close of the novel — alone, returned to the work, to the school, to the mission of training other women.
Now — is that a triumph or a defeat?
Gissing, to his great credit, refuses to tell us.
That ambiguity is, I would argue, the mark of a serious novelist rather than a propagandist.
I think Edmund is right that the ending is deliberately ambivalent — but I read the ambivalence differently.
Rhoda returns to the school, yes — but Monica is dead, Virginia is destroyed by drink, Widdowson is a ruin.
The reform project is still standing, but it is standing in a landscape of wreckage.
Gissing is saying: the school is necessary, the work is necessary — and it is not enough.
The women who most needed the escape hatch were the ones the hatch was too small and too late to save.
What I find shattering — and I mean that precisely — is the death of Monica's child and the disposal of Monica herself.
She dies unreconciled with Widdowson, having never been truly known by anyone in the novel.
Gissing doesn't give her a redemptive deathbed scene — she is simply consumed and gone.
In the great tradition of Victorian fiction, that refusal of consolation is itself a kind of moral statement — possibly the novel's most honest one.
A novel that refuses easy consolation at every turn — and that includes, perhaps, how it chooses to narrate its own horrors.
Which leads us, naturally, to Gissing's narrative voice itself — the way the novel watches its characters with that cool, slightly unsettling ironic distance.

segments.title: The Narrative Voice and Gissing's Ironic Distance

utterances.text: We've been talking about the walls that hem these characters in — social, economic, institutional.
But there's another presence in this novel that shapes everything we receive: the narrator himself.
Gissing's narrative voice is one of the strangest and most controlled instruments in Victorian fiction.
So let's turn to the question of how Gissing tells this story — and what that telling does to us as readers.
The first thing you notice, reading this novel aloud — and I've spent considerable time in its company — is that the narrator almost never raises his voice.
There are no exclamations, no authorial laments about the cruelty of fate.
The prose proceeds with this extraordinary, almost clinical steadiness.
And yet the irony is absolutely devastating — it's just delivered very quietly.
Think of the opening chapters — the Madden girls being assessed, essentially, like livestock at a market.
Gissing describes their upbringing, their father's cheerful uselessness, their complete lack of preparation for independent life.
And the tone is so level, so measured — that levelness IS the indictment.
I think one must be careful not to read every instance of narrative restraint as ideological accusation.
There is a long tradition in English prose — going back at least to Fielding — of the narrator who maintains composure precisely because the subject matter is distressing.
What Gissing is doing, I'd suggest, is closer to a kind of stoic witness.
He sees clearly; he records faithfully; he does not editorialise, because to editorialise would be to reduce the dignity of what he's observing.
That said, Oliver is right that the irony is present — it operates through juxtaposition rather than explicit comment.
When Rhoda Nunn speaks with such vigour about the emancipated woman, and we are shown Monica's quiet, crumbling hopes in the very next scene — that arrangement is the argument.
I want to take that a step further.
Gissing's ironic distance isn't just a stylistic preference — it's a structural response to an impossible position.
He is a man writing about women's oppression with genuine sympathy, but also with the consciousness that he is an outsider to that experience.
The distance is partly ethical — he won't presume to speak from inside a suffering he hasn't lived.
But it also produces something remarkable: the narrator becomes a kind of camera that catches what the characters cannot say about themselves.
Consider how he handles Widdowson — that portrait of masculine anxiety dressed up as protective love.
Widdowson himself believes he loves Monica deeply and unselfishly.
The narrator simply shows us what that love looks like in practice — the surveillance, the curtailed freedoms, the slow suffocation.
No verdict is delivered. None is needed.
That Widdowson business is some of the most chilling writing in the novel, precisely because of that restraint Daniel describes.
There's a passage where Widdowson follows Monica through London — literally trails her through the streets.
And Gissing writes something to the effect that Widdowson told himself this was the natural concern of a devoted husband.
That phrase — 'told himself' — is doing an enormous amount of work.
The gap between what a character tells himself and what the reader sees — that's where Gissing lives as a novelist.
He's doing something that won't really get named until Freud comes along and gives it vocabulary.
I wouldn't want to anachronise Gissing into a proto-Freudian, tempting as that is.
What Gissing is doing is older and, in some ways, more demanding than free indirect discourse.
He is holding characters morally accountable — in the classical sense — for the stories they tell about their own motives.
That is fundamentally a moral exercise, not a psychological one.
The narrator's irony is a form of judgement — it insists that self-deception is a choice, even when the social pressures are real.
That, I think, is why Everard Barfoot is such a fascinating study.
He is intelligent enough to articulate a progressive position on women's freedom, and yet the narrator quietly tracks every place where his behaviour contradicts it.
Barfoot is the novel's most sophisticated ideological trap.
He talks the language of liberation — he wants Rhoda to live with him without marriage, to prove the freedom of the arrangement.
But the narrator keeps showing us that the risk of that arrangement falls entirely on Rhoda, not on him.
He has property, mobility, reputation that is essentially indestructible.
She has — what?
Her work, her standing at the typewriting school, the one thing she's built by her own will.
And all of that is what she stakes.
Gissing's narrator sees this asymmetry with perfect clarity — and never once points at it directly.
The reader does the pointing.
That's the genius of it, isn't it — Gissing implicates the reader in the act of judgement.
You can't read passively. The prose demands that you complete the moral circuit.
And Rhoda herself is the hardest case — because the narrator applies the same ironic distance to her as to everyone else.
Her certainties are not spared.
When she lectures poor Monica about the necessity of independence, there's a slight thinness to the rhetoric the narrator allows us to hear.
As if even the most sympathetically presented programme in the novel is being held at arm's length and examined.
Nobody in this book gets to be simply right.
That evenhandedness is what separates Gissing from the pamphleteers of his era.
He doesn't spare Miss Nunn's rigidities any more than he spares Widdowson's possessiveness.
Mary Barfoot, who is perhaps the most intellectually admirable figure in the novel, is nonetheless observed with a certain gentle scepticism.
Her speeches to the young women at the school are passionate and intelligent — and yet the narrator does not ask us to bow before them.
I think this reflects Gissing's deepest artistic conviction: that the novel is not a vehicle for solutions.
It is a vehicle for seeing — seeing clearly, and bearing what one sees.
I'll grant that — up to a point.
The ironic distance does produce that sense of unflinching witness Edmund describes.
But I'd argue that Gissing's irony has a political direction even when it doesn't have a political prescription.
The suffering in this novel is not distributed randomly.
It concentrates in women, in the poor, in those without the structural advantages of property and sex.
The narrator's cool eye is trained, as if by instinct, on exactly those concentrations.
You can call that stoic witness if you like.
I call it an anatomy of a system, conducted with surgical precision and a great deal of suppressed rage.
A stoic witness — or a suppressed rage.
Perhaps those two readings aren't as incompatible as they sound — Gissing seems to hold both in tension deliberately.
What we've been circling is the question of whether this novel offers any reckoning — any final accounting — for all that it so dispassionately records.
That's exactly where we'll go next — to the tyranny of circumstance, and what, if anything, Gissing allows his characters by way of resolution.

segments.title: The Tyranny of Circumstance: Synthesis and Reckoning

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Gissing's narrative voice holds its characters at a certain ironic distance — observing, recording, never quite sentimentalising.
That distance, I think, brings us to the hardest question the novel poses: who is actually responsible for the suffering we witness?
Is it individual weakness, is it society, is it simply the brute weight of circumstance — the tyranny, as Gissing might say, of the way things are?
I think Gissing is absolutely clear on this, even if he refuses to be polemical about it.
The Madden sisters at the beginning of the novel — they are not destroyed by moral failure.
They are destroyed by the death of their father, a man who never thought to educate them for independence, who assumed the world would always provide a husband.
That structural vulnerability — that's not personal weakness, that is a system designed to keep women dependent.
Gissing shows us the mechanism with almost clinical precision.
I won't dispute the mechanism, but I do resist the conclusion that mechanism is the whole story.
Consider Rhoda Nunn — she inhabits the same world, the same constraints, and she forges something extraordinary from them.
Her will, her discipline, her refusal to be absorbed into domestic subordination — these are qualities of character, not merely of circumstance.
Gissing admires her, I think — genuinely admires her — and the admiration is for what she has made of herself.
But then Gissing does something rather cruel to Rhoda, doesn't he.
He sends Everard Barfoot into her orbit — that brilliant, infuriating, genuinely compelling man — and watches what happens to her certainties.
She comes so very close to surrendering the whole project — not because she's weak, but because Gissing understands that strength is not armour.
And there's that marvellous, devastating moment near the end when she says she is glad — glad — that she did not marry him.
Whether she believes it is another question entirely.
And that ambiguity is where Gissing is most honest, I think — more honest than he perhaps intended to be.
Because what he's showing us is that even the most conscious, most principled resistance can be eroded — not by wickedness, but by longing.
Monica Widdowson is the counterexample he sets beside Rhoda — and Monica's fate is the novel's most brutal argument.
She marries to escape the draper's shop, escapes into something worse, and then finds no exit at all — she dies in childbed, and the child dies with her.
Gissing doesn't editorialize — he simply places the consequence before us and lets it stand.
Monica is the most genuinely tragic figure in the novel precisely because she is neither villain nor fool.
She is simply a young woman of ordinary gifts and ordinary hopes who is placed in a position that requires extraordinary virtue to survive.
That is the classical definition of tragedy — not the defeat of the wicked, but the destruction of the merely human.
Widdowson himself — I find him one of the most psychologically complete portraits of tyranny in Victorian fiction.
He is not a monster — he is a man who loves his wife and cannot conceive that love might require relinquishing control.
Widdowson is one of those characters who is absolutely chilling precisely because he's so recognisable.
His surveillance of Monica — following her through London, timing her movements, his jealousy dressed in the language of concern — it reads like a contemporary case study.
And yet Gissing won't quite let us hate him without complication.
He shows us how Widdowson arrived at this state — a man of leisure, of no real purpose, who has poured the entirety of his emotional life into one vessel.
That's not exculpation — but it is understanding, and Gissing is always more interested in understanding than in judgment.
What's striking to me is that Gissing gives us Mary Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn as this alternative — a world of work, purpose, solidarity — and he doesn't romanticise it either.
Their school for typewriting, their mission — it's admirable, and it's also fragile, and sometimes rather bleak.
Does the novel ultimately believe in the project it's describing?
I think it believes in it the way a doctor believes in a treatment that may not be enough — with commitment, but without illusion.
Mary Barfoot's speeches to her students — there's a remarkable moment where she tells them that the old idea of womanhood is an insult, and the new one requires courage.
Gissing gives her that rhetoric and means it — but then he places it against the material reality of what these women face.
Rhetoric alone will not pay the rent — and Gissing knows it, and so does Mary Barfoot.
Mary Barfoot is perhaps the most fully realised idealist in the novel — and Gissing grants her that stature without making her a mouthpiece.
She has doubts, she has passions of her own — her feeling for Everard Barfoot has that slightly suppressed intensity that Gissing handles so well.
What I find admirable in Gissing is that he does not require his characters to be consistent — only to be human.
And that, I would argue, is the mark of genuine moral imagination — as opposed to the programmatic imagination of the social tract.
I keep coming back to the ending — which is one of the most interesting endings in Victorian fiction, precisely because it refuses consolation.
Rhoda holds the infant — Monica's child, the child who will live — and the novel's last image is of this woman who chose independence, holding the fruit of another woman's ruin.
It doesn't resolve anything — it simply places those two facts side by side and trusts us to feel the weight.
That's Gissing at his very finest — when he stops explaining and simply shows.
And the child is a girl — Gissing specifies that — and Rhoda determines that she will grow up differently.
That tiny detail carries the entire argument of the novel forward into the future — this is what the odd women are working toward.
Not utopia — just the possibility that the next generation might inherit something better than a system designed to break them.
I would say Gissing's final gesture is one of guarded hope rather than hope itself — which is perhaps the most honest position available to a man of his temperament and his era.
He looked at the world as it was — not as reformers wished it to be — and he recorded what he saw with complete fidelity.
That is an achievement of the first order, whatever one thinks of his conclusions.
I think that's exactly right — and it's why the novel still has this quality of pressing on the reader, of refusing to let us off easily.
The odd women of the title — those surplus women for whom Victorian society had no plan — Gissing makes them the measure of everything the world got wrong.
And in Rhoda Nunn he gives us one answer to how a person might live inside that wrongness with dignity and purpose — though not without cost.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, to Sir Edmund Leigh, and to Daniel Rosen — three readers who have brought this novel alive today with quite exceptional generosity and insight.

We've ranged across the novel's world — the draper's shop, the typewriting school, the grim marriages and the fragile freedoms — and I hope we've done some justice to a writer who deserves far more attention than he usually receives.
Thank you for listening to The Odd Women Unpacked.

c22:p1.text:
Tremor of self-consciousness kept Monica in dread of being watched and
suspected. Few people were present to-day, and after exchanging formal
words with Bevis, she moved away to talk with the hostess. Not till
half an hour had passed did she venture to obey the glances which her
all but avowed lover cast towards her in conversation. He was so much
at ease, so like what she had always known him, that Monica asked
herself whether she had not mistaken the meaning of his homage. One
moment she hoped it might be so; the next, she longed for some sign of
passionate devotion, and thought with anguish of the day, now so near,
when he would be gone for ever. This, she ardently believed, was the
man who should have been her husband. Him she could love with heart and
soul, could make his will her absolute law, could live on his smiles,
could devote herself to his interests. The independence she had been
struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to
love. If she had understood herself as she now did, her life would
never have been thus cast into bondage.
c22:p1.summary: Monica's self-consciousness masks her longing for Bevis, whom she believes she truly loves and could devote herself to completely, unlike her constrained marriage.
c22:p1.best_quote: The independence she had been struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to love.

matched_quotes.text: The dread of an unoccupied future was one of the results of her education.

c15:p118.text:
Yet a feeling of inability to grapple with such an undertaking as this
grew on him the more he thought of it. Naturally, his mind busied
itself with such vague knowledge as he had gathered of those places in
the South of France, where rich English people go to escape their own
climate: Nice, Cannes. He could not imagine himself setting forth to
these regions. Doubtless it was possible to travel thither, and live
there when one arrived, without a knowledge of French; but he pictured
all sorts of humiliating situations resulting from his ignorance. Above
everything he dreaded humiliation in Monica’s sight; it would be
intolerable to have her comparing him with men who spoke foreign
languages, and were at home on the Continent.
c15:p118.summary: Widdowson's growing anxiety focuses on his fear of humiliation in Monica's sight; he dreads her comparing him unfavorably to cosmopolitan men.
c15:p118.best_quote: Above everything he dreaded humiliation in Monica's sight; it would be intolerable to have her comparing him with men who spoke foreign languages, and were at home on the Continent.

matched_quotes.text: Gissing phrases it with characteristic bluntness: 'I thought I was above such weaknesses.

c6:p102.text:
“Personal feeling is misleading you,” Rhoda pursued. “Miss Royston had
a certain cleverness, I grant; but do you think I didn’t know that she
would never become what you hoped? All her spare time was given to
novel-reading. If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the
sea we should have some chance of reforming women. The girl’s nature
was corrupted with sentimentality, like that of all but every woman who
is intelligent enough to read what is called the best fiction, but not
intelligent enough to understand its vice. Love—love—love; a
sickening sameness of vulgarity. What is more vulgar than the ideal of
novelists? They won’t represent the actual world; it would be too dull
for their readers. In real life, how many men and women  fall in love ?
Not one in every ten thousand, I am convinced. Not one married pair in
ten thousand have felt for each other as two or three couples do in
every novel. There is the sexual instinct, of course, but that is quite
a different thing; the novelists daren’t talk about that. The paltry
creatures daren’t tell the one truth that would be profitable. The
result is that women imagine themselves noble and glorious when they
are most near the animals. This Miss Royston—when she rushed off to
perdition, ten to one she had in mind some idiot heroine of a book. Oh,
I tell you that you are losing sight of your first duty. There are
people enough to act the good Samaritan;  you  have quite another task
in life. It is your work to train and encourage girls in a path as far
as possible from that of the husband-hunter. Let them marry later, if
they must; but at all events you will have cleared their views on the
subject of marriage, and put them in a position to judge the man who
offers himself. You will have taught them that marriage is an alliance
of intellects—not a means of support, or something more ignoble still.
But to do this with effect you must show yourself relentless to female
imbecility. If a girl gets to know that you have received back such a
person as Miss Royston she will be corrupted by your spirit of
charity—corrupted, at all events, for our purposes. The endeavour to
give women a new soul is so difficult that we can’t be cumbered by
side-tasks, such as fishing foolish people out of the mud they have
walked into. Charity for human weakness is all very well in its place,
but it is precisely one of the virtues that you must  not  teach. You
have to set an example of the sterner qualities—to discourage anything
that resembles sentimentalism. And think if you illustrate in your own
behaviour a sympathy for the very vice of character we are trying our
hardest to extirpate!”
c6:p102.summary: Rhoda argues that Bella was corrupted by sentimental novels that misrepresent love; she attacks sentimentality and the romantic ideal as enemies of female progress; warns that readmitting Bella would teach charity instead of the stern virtues needed for true emancipation.
c6:p102.best_quote: If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the sea we should have some chance of reforming women.

matched_quotes.text: She speaks of women who are taught that marriage is the one respectable goal, and who are therefore helpless when marriage fails or never arrives.

c26:p28.text:
“My DEAR RHODA,—I have just gone through a very painful scene, and I
feel bound to let you know of it without delay, as it  may  concern
you. This evening (Monday), when I came home from Great Portland
Street, Emma told me that Mr. Widdowson had called, that he wished to
see me as soon as possible, and would be here again at six o’clock. He
came, and his appearance alarmed me, he was looking so dreadfully ill.
Without preface, he said, “My wife has left me; she has gone to her
sister, and refuses to return.” This was astonishing in itself, and I
wondered still more why he should come and tell  me  about it in so
strange a way. The explanation followed very promptly, and you may
judge how I heard it. Mr. Widdowson said that his wife had been
behaving very badly of late; that he had discovered several falsehoods
she had told him as to her employment during absences from home, in
daytime and evening. Having cause for suspecting the worst, he last
Saturday engaged a private detective to follow Mrs. Widdowson wherever
she went. This man saw her go to the flats in Bayswater where Everard
lives and knock at  his  door. As no one replied, she went away for a
time and returned, but again found no one at home. This being at once
reported to Mr. Widdowson he asked his wife where she had been that
afternoon. The answer was false; she said she had been here, with me.
Thereupon he lost command of himself, and charged her with infidelity.
She refused to offer any kind of explanation, but denied that she was
guilty and at once left the house. Since, she has utterly refused to
see him. Her sister can only report that Monica is very ill, and that
she charges her husband with accusing her falsely.
c26:p28.summary: Mary recounts Edmund Widdowson's distressing visit: he has hired a detective who observed Monica visiting Everard's flat, leading Edmund to accuse Monica of infidelity; Monica has left him.
c26:p28.best_quote: My wife has left me; she has gone to her sister, and refuses to return.

matched_quotes.text: And Gissing writes something to the effect that Widdowson told himself this was the natural concern of a devoted husband.

c12:p83.text:
It was with no little curiosity that, on the appointed morning, Barfoot
repaired to South Tottenham. He had seen a photograph of Miss Wheatley,
but it dated from seventeen years ago. Standing in her presence, he was
moved with compassion, and with another feeling more rarely excited in
him by a woman’s face, that of reverential tenderness. Impossible to
recognize in this countenance the features known to him from the
portrait. At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple
comeliness on which any man’s eye would have rested with pleasure; at
forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness
stamped upon her brow and lips. She looked much older than Mary
Barfoot, though they were just of an age. And all this for want of a
little money. The life of a pure, gentle, tender-hearted woman worn
away in hopeless longing and in hard struggle for daily bread. As she
took his hand and thanked him with an exquisite modesty for the present
she had received, Everard felt a lump rise in his throat. He was
ashamed to notice that the years had dealt so unkindly with her; fixing
his look upon her eyes, he gladdened at the gladness which shone in
them, at the soft light which they could still shed forth.
c12:p83.summary: On the wedding morning, Everard observes Fanny for the first time; her face is ravaged by years of poverty and privation; she looks much older than Mary Barfoot despite being her age. Everard is moved to tears by her modesty and the tragedy of her sacrificed life, yet her eyes still shine with gladness and tenderness.
c12:p83.best_quote: At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple comeliness on which any man's eye would have rested with pleasure; at forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness stamped upon her brow and lips.

c13:p39.text:
“If I  must  satisfy your curiosity, Mr. Barfoot, I had better tell you
at once that the subject of our difference is the girl you mentioned.
Not very long ago she tried to persuade your cousin to receive her
again—to give her lessons at the place in Great Portland Street, as
before she disgraced herself. Miss Barfoot, with too ready good-nature,
was willing to do this, but I resisted. It seemed to me that it would
be a very weak and wrong thing to do. At the time she ended by agreeing
with me. Now that the girl has killed herself, she throws the blame
upon my interference. We had a painful conversation, and I don’t think
we can continue to live together.”
c13:p39.summary: Rhoda explains that Mary wanted to re-hire Bella Royston, but Rhoda opposed it as a sign of moral weakness; after Bella's suicide, Mary blames Rhoda's interference for the tragedy.
c13:p39.best_quote: the subject of our difference is the girl you mentioned... It seemed to me that it would be a very weak and wrong thing to do

c13:p76.text:
Enough for the present. Having raised his hat and turned on his heels,
Barfoot strolled away in a mood of peculiar satisfaction. He laughed to
himself. She was certainly a fine creature—yes, physically as well.
Her out-of-door appearance on the whole pleased him; she could dress
very plainly without disguising the advantages of figure she possessed.
He pictured her rambling about the hills, and longed to be her
companion on such an expedition; there would be no consulting with
feebleness, as when one sets forth to walk with the everyday woman.
What daring topics might come up in the course of a twenty-mile stretch
across country! No Grundyism in Rhoda Nunn; no simpering, no mincing of
phrases. Why, a man might do worse than secure her for his comrade
through the whole journey of life.
c13:p76.summary: Everard walks away satisfied, picturing Rhoda as a remarkable woman—intellectually and physically appealing—and fantasizes about her as a companion through life, admiring her lack of conventional femininity.
c13:p76.best_quote: Why, a man might do worse than secure her for his comrade through the whole journey of life

c1:p31.text:
The dialogue out in the passage was brief. A messenger had just arrived
with the tidings that Dr. Madden, driving back from Kingston Seymour,
had been thrown from his vehicle and lay insensible at a roadside
cottage.
c1:p31.summary: A messenger brings news that Dr. Madden has been thrown from his carriage while returning home and lies unconscious at a cottage.
c1:p31.best_quote: "A messenger had just arrived with the tidings that Dr. Madden, driving back from Kingston Seymour, had been thrown from his vehicle and lay insensible at a roadside cottage."

c11:p35.text:
“MY DEAREST MONICA,”—the missive began—“Why have you not written
before this? I have been dreadfully uneasy ever since receiving your
last letter. Your headache soon went away, I hope? Why haven’t you made
another appointment? It is all I can do to keep from breaking my
promise and coming to ask about you. Write at once, I implore you, my
dearest. It’s no use telling me that I must not use these words of
affection; they come to my lips and to my pen irresistibly. You know so
well that I love you with all my heart and soul; I can’t address you
like I did when we first corresponded. My darling! My dear, sweet,
beautiful little girl—”
c11:p35.summary: Widdowson's letter expresses overwhelming love and longing for Monica, with escalating passionate language and reproaches for her silence, revealing his emotional desperation and intensity.
c11:p35.best_quote: My darling! My dear, sweet, beautiful little girl—

c11:p105.summary: Monica announces to her sister that she is going to be married.
c11:p105.best_quote: Virgie—I am going to be married

c24:p11.text:
Her moods alternated with distracting rapidity. A hundred times she had
resolved that Bevis could be nothing more to her, and again had thought
of him with impulses of yearning, trying to persuade herself that he
had acted well and wisely. A hundred times she determined to carry out
her idea of yesterday—to quit her husband and resist all his efforts
to recall her—and again had all but resigned herself to live with him,
accepting degradation as so many wives perforce did. Her mind was in
confusion, and physically she felt far from well. A heaviness weighed
upon her limbs, making it hardship to walk however short a distance.
c24:p11.summary: Monica's mind swings wildly between rejecting Bevis and longing for him, between leaving her husband and accepting her degradation as a wife.
c24:p11.best_quote: A hundred times she had resolved that Bevis could be nothing more to her, and again had thought of him with impulses of yearning, trying to persuade herself that he had acted well and wisely.

c24:p13.text:
She came out of the shop with flushed cheeks. Another step in shameful
descent—yet it had the result of strengthening once more her emotions
favourable to Bevis. On his account she had braved this ignominy, and
it drew her towards him, instead of producing the effect which would
have seemed more natural. Perhaps the reason was that she felt herself
more hopelessly an outcast from the world of honourable women, and
therefore longed in her desolation for the support of a man’s love. Did
he not love her? It was  her  fault if she expected him to act with a
boldness that did not lie in his nature. Perhaps his discretion, which
she had so bitterly condemned as weakness, meant a wise regard for her
interests as well as his own. The public scandal of divorce was a
hideous thing. If it damaged his prospects and sundered him from his
relatives, how could she hope that his love of her, the cause of it
all, would long endure?
c24:p13.summary: Monica rationalizes her attraction to Bevis after her act of shame, seeing his discretion as wise protection and fearing the scandal of divorce.
c24:p13.best_quote: Perhaps the reason was that she felt herself more hopelessly an outcast from the world of honourable women, and therefore longed in her desolation for the support of a man's love.

c24:p25.text:
Self-torment of every kind was natural to her position. Though the
relief of escaping from several distinct dangers had put her mind
comparatively at ease for a short time, she had now begun to suffer a
fresh uneasiness with reference to the young and handsome woman who
came downstairs. The fact that no one answered the workman’s knock had
seemed to her a sufficient proof that Bevis was not at home, and that
the stranger must have come forth from the flat opposite his. But she
recollected the incident which had so alarmingly disturbed her and her
lover yesterday. Bevis did not then go to the door, and suppose—oh, it
was folly! But suppose that woman had been with him; suppose he did not
care to open to a visitor whose signal sounded only a minute or two
after that person’s departure?
c24:p25.summary: Monica torments herself imagining that the woman descending the stairs was Bevis's lover, despite her attempts to dismiss the idea.
c24:p25.best_quote: But she recollected the incident which had so alarmingly disturbed her and her lover yesterday. Bevis did not then go to the door, and suppose—oh, it was folly! But suppose that woman had been with him; suppose he did not care to open to a visitor whose signal sounded only a minute or two after that person's departure?
